name: Hope David Michael
feedback: D1: You catalogued seven of the ten findings with quoted source lines and reconciled capture timestamps, and that evidence discipline is the strongest part of this deliverable. SQL injection (A03/CWE-89, lines 62-67, capture 02:15:31), JWT alg:none (A07/CWE-347, Token 2), XXE (A05/CWE-611), path traversal (A01/CWE-22, /files/?path=/etc/passwd at 02:24:02) and open redirect (A01/CWE-601, 02:21:13) are all correct and well sourced, and CWE-327 for the unsalted MD5 is a defensible variant of CWE-916. The decoy work is excellent: you named the tempting hand-rolled b64url helpers, proved them sound against RFC 7515 at the mechanism level, and correctly kept alg:none as a real bug rather than mislabelling it the decoy, so you earned full decoy credit. What cost you was three missing findings: the hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (CWE-798, ~line 30/38), the absent token expiry (CWE-613, ~74-75) and the cookie missing Secure and SameSite (CWE-614, ~86). Also note finding 03 is a STORED XSS in comments (the cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443 at 02:18:47), not reflected, even though your evidence line was right. D2: The hops you presented are correct and carry verbatim PoC, the SQLi request, the full forged alg:none token, and the complete XXE XML body, which is exactly what graders want to see. The chain is too compressed though; you collapsed it to four hops and dropped the stored XSS (02:18:47) and open redirect (02:21:13) hops that sit between auth bypass and file read, so the in-order reconciliation is incomplete. Your CVSS strings are complete vectors but they sit bare in a table with no justifying sentence each, and the SQLi vector should be AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1, not A:H, because the login bypass does not hit availability. You also missed the senior insight that the forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service, which is a scope change to S:C. Your impact section is the highlight here: 312 records, an average-balance assumption stated openly, about 55M NGN of direct exposure and the BoltCash launch tie are all reasoned rather than asserted. D3: This is your best deliverable. The executive summary lands on 312 customer records and the BoltCash risk, the threat model is present, the findings table ties to evidence, and you restated the disproved decoy correctly. Most importantly your remediation table is genuinely ordered by Risk Reduction per Hour and effort, XXE first because it is low effort, MD5 last because it is very high effort, which is the effort-to-risk reasoning the brief asks for rather than blind CVSS ordering. Both detection stopgaps are deployable with exact patterns, target fields and false-positive rates (<0.1% for the XXE WAF rule, <1% for the SQLi/traversal SIEM alert). To push this higher, name the earliest-break fix explicitly: the SQLi at login is the root entry, so the prepared-statement fix is the single hop that breaks the whole chain. D4: You answered all four prompts in your own voice with a clear owned decision, declined the journalist cleanly, refused to bury the console-timeline evidence, and made breach notification the non-negotiable action. ISC2 Canon 1 is cited by number and is load-bearing in your argument. The one real slip is the NDPA section: the 72-hour duty to notify the NDPC is Section 40, and Section 41 covers notifying affected data subjects on high risk, not Section 30, so cite those and tie them to the 312 customers. I looked for a way to round this up into the 70s and the missing three D1 findings, the two dropped chain hops and the unjustified CVSS vectors genuinely do not support it. The single most important fix: catalogue all ten findings with quoted lines and reconcile every chain hop in order, because a partial catalogue and a compressed chain are what separate this from a high-70s report.
